section.title: Advanced Payload
section.description: Seventeen UI/UX lessons that build real components and responsive charts with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: relationships, blocks, arrays, access control, versions, live preview, and a learner-published showcase.

lessons.title: Components, two worlds
lessons.outcome: Tell the difference between a Payload admin component and a public frontend component, and choose the right rendering boundary.
mental_model: **Payload renders two surfaces.** The admin panel is a React/Next app you can replace piece by piece; your public frontend is a separate React surface that reads Payload data.
**Server Components are the default.** Add `'use client'` only when a component needs state, event handlers, effects, or browser APIs.
**Data flows one way.** Payload stores content and exposes it through the Local API or REST; your components decide how that content becomes UI.

lab.title: Build the bridge card
lab.brief: Start with a plain card. Give it a clear hierarchy, one action, and enough space to breathe. Then publish it to the showcase.
checklist: The headline is the first thing you read
The body copy supports the headline
There is one obvious action
The action is reachable with the keyboard
The card still works at 360px wide
hints: Use the eyebrow for context, not a second headline.
A short body is easier to scan than a paragraph.
Use min-height on the action so it has a comfortable hit area.
Publish after saving and confirm the card appears in the gallery.

lessons.takeaway: Know which surface you are building on before you write the component; the rendering boundary is an architectural decision.

knowledge_check.question: Which component needs the 'use client' directive?
options: A card that only renders text and links
A form that tracks input and handles submit
A server component that queries the Local API
knowledge_check.explanation: Client components are required for state, event handlers, effects, and browser APIs. Static rendering and server-side data fetching can stay on the server.

deep_dive.title: Admin vs frontend
deep_dive.body: Admin components live under admin.components and render inside Payload. Frontend components live in your app and receive Payload data as props. They can share a design language, but they are different surfaces.

deep_dive.title: Server vs client
deep_dive.body: Server Components can query the Local API directly and keep secrets on the server. Client Components receive serializable props and run in the browser. Move the boundary down the tree when only a small part needs interactivity.

deep_dive.title: Component paths
deep_dive.body: Payload does not import admin components directly into the config. It resolves a file path through the generated import map, so a typo becomes a build-time problem you can catch early.

lessons.title: Design tokens as data
lessons.outcome: Model a small token contract in Payload and render every component from the same variables.
mental_model: **Tokens are the contract.** Color, radius, spacing, type scale, and elevation are data, not one-off styles.
**CSS variables are the bridge.** Payload stores values; React writes them onto a wrapper; CSS consumes them.
**Theme is a token, not a second stylesheet.** A light/dark switch should change values, not fork every component.

lab.title: Tune a token-driven button
lab.brief: Build the primary action with CSS custom properties. The same button should cover default, hover, active, focus-visible, disabled, and busy states.
checklist: At least 44px tall
Hover and active feedback
Visible focus-visible ring
Disabled state is readable
Accent and text pass contrast
hints: Use spacing to reach the hit area instead of a larger font.
Declare the token contract on :root, then consume it with var().
A ghost button needs a visible boundary on focus.
Set aria-busy while the action is running so the state is announced.

lessons.takeaway: A small, explicit token contract keeps every component consistent without duplicating CSS.

knowledge_check.question: Why store design tokens in Payload instead of hard-coding them in each component?
options: It makes the components render faster
It gives every component one source of truth for visual decisions
It removes the need for CSS
knowledge_check.explanation: Tokens create a shared contract. Changing a value in Payload updates every component that consumes the same variables, while contrast still needs to be tested.

deep_dive.title: The token contract
deep_dive.body: Start with the decisions every component shares: accent, background, foreground, muted text, radius, spacing, type scale, and shadow. Add more only when a real component needs them.

deep_dive.title: Payload admin variables
deep_dive.body: Payload exposes its own CSS variables for the admin panel, such as elevation and theme colors. Custom admin components can use them so they adapt to the active theme automatically.

deep_dive.title: Contrast is not automatic
deep_dive.body: A beautiful accent can still fail contrast. Check text on the background and the action label on the accent; aim for 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text and UI boundaries.

lessons.title: Accessible primitives
lessons.outcome: Build a form that works with a keyboard, a screen reader, and a thumb.
mental_model: **Labels are part of the control.** A placeholder is an example, not a label.
**Focus is a state.** `:focus-visible` tells keyboard users where they are without flashing a ring on every click.
**Feedback closes the loop.** A success or error message must be text, associated with the field, and announced.

lab.title: Build the contact form
lab.brief: Add visible labels, the right input types, required fields, and a success message that does not reload the page. Test the form with the keyboard.
checklist: Every field has a visible label
Email uses type=email
Required fields are marked
Submit shows a success message
Keyboard focus is visible
hints: Connect each label with for and id.
Use autocomplete=name and autocomplete=email.
role="status" announces the success message without stealing focus.
Keep the form markup semantic: form, label, input, textarea, button.

lessons.takeaway: Accessibility is not a final pass; it is the shape of the primitive itself.

knowledge_check.question: Which attributes connect a label to an input?
knowledge_check.explanation: The label's for attribute must match the input's id. Clicking the label then focuses the input, and screen readers announce them together.

deep_dive.title: Labels vs placeholders
deep_dive.body: A placeholder disappears after typing and cannot be relied on as a label. Keep a visible label above the field and use the placeholder for an example.

deep_dive.title: Focus-visible
deep_dive.body: Use `:focus-visible` for the keyboard ring. It keeps the pointer experience clean while giving keyboard users a clear target. Never remove focus outlines without a replacement.

deep_dive.title: Status messages
deep_dive.body: A `role="status"` element announces polite updates such as “Message sent.” For errors, associate the message with the field and mark the field invalid.

lessons.title: Custom admin components
lessons.outcome: Replace a piece of the Payload admin with your own React component and keep the server/client boundary intact.
mental_model: **`admin.components` is the extension point.** Root views, collection views, fields, and login screens all accept your components.
**Server components get the payload instance.** They can query the Local API and render data without a client round trip.
**Client components get serializable props.** Add `'use client'` only for interaction, and never pass secrets or the full config across the boundary.

lab.brief: Design a small card for the Payload dashboard. It should answer one question and link to the collection behind it. This lab is a visual prototype: real Payload admin views are React components.

No action is hidden behind a hover
hints: Use the accent for the trend, not the whole card.
Keep the label and footnote quiet.

lessons.takeaway: Admin customization is real application code: keep it small, server-first, and focused on the editor's job.

knowledge_check.question: Where do you register a custom Payload dashboard view?
knowledge_check.explanation: Root views are registered under `admin.components.views`. The dashboard key replaces the default dashboard with your component path.

deep_dive.title: Component paths and the import map
deep_dive.body: Payload resolves custom components by file path, then generates an import map at `app/(payload)/admin/importMap.js`. Paths are relative to `admin.importMap.baseDir`, and named exports use a `#ExportName` suffix.

deep_dive.title: Server props
deep_dive.body: Root views receive `initPageResult`, which includes `req`, `payload`, and `permissions`. Use `req.user` for access checks and the read-filtered `user` for anything you render or pass to a client component.

deep_dive.title: Performance
deep_dive.body: Server components stream less JavaScript to the browser. Keep the client boundary small, memoize expensive work, and use `useFormFields` instead of `useFields` when you only need one field.

lessons.title: Custom field components
lessons.outcome: Build a field component that reads and writes a Payload field value without breaking the form contract.
mental_model: **The field owns value and change.** A custom field must call `setValue`; otherwise Payload never sees the edit.
**`useField` is the bridge.** It gives a client component the value and setter for its path.
**Validation belongs on the server.** UI hints help, but the field config and access control are the real boundary.

lab.title: Build a color token field
lab.brief: Create the field an editor uses to set the accent token. It needs a swatch, a hex value, a helper line, and a live preview. Real Payload field components are React; this lab prototypes the control.
checklist: The control has a visible label
A swatch and hex value stay in sync
Helper text explains where the token is used
The control is keyboard reachable
The value is valid before save
hints: Use type=color for the picker and a text input for the hex value.
Validate with a hex pattern before updating the preview.
The helper text is part of the field, not decoration.
Use aria-invalid and a status message for invalid input.

starter.html: Used for primary actions and focus rings.

solution.html: Used for primary actions and focus rings.

lessons.takeaway: A custom field is a form control with a contract: render the value, emit the change, and leave authorization to the server.

knowledge_check.question: Which hook reads and writes a field value inside a client field component?
knowledge_check.explanation: `useField` returns the current value and `setValue` for the field at the supplied path. `useFormFields` is better when you only need to subscribe to one value without the setter.

deep_dive.title: useField vs useFormFields
deep_dive.body: `useField` is for the field's own control. `useFormFields` subscribes to one value from the whole form and is useful for conditional UI without re-rendering on every keystroke.

deep_dive.title: Field access vs validation
deep_dive.body: Field access decides who can read or update a value. Validation decides whether the value is acceptable. They solve different problems; a custom UI does not replace either.

deep_dive.title: Cells and filters
deep_dive.body: A field can also provide custom `Cell` and `Filter` components for the list view. Keep those lightweight and consistent with the edit control's vocabulary.

lessons.title: Blocks and the page builder
lessons.outcome: Model a page as reusable blocks and render it with a one-to-one React registry.
mental_model: **Blocks are typed rows.** Each block has a `blockType` and its own fields; the array preserves order.
**One block, one renderer.** A registry maps `blockType` to a component, so adding a block is a schema change plus a renderer.
**Structure stays in the CMS.** Editors compose and reorder; developers keep the rendering predictable.

lab.title: Compose a page from blocks
lab.brief: Build a page from distinct sections: a hero, a feature grid, a testimonial, and a call to action. Each block should stand on its own and survive a narrow screen.

The page follows a readable order
The feature grid wraps at 360px
The call to action is obvious
Every section has semantic markup
hints: Use section elements with aria-labelledby for each block.
A feature grid can be one rule: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr)).
Keep one block, one visual idea.
Publish after saving and check the page preview in the showcase.

knowledge_check.question: What identifies which schema a saved block uses?
knowledge_check.explanation: Payload stores `blockType` using the block's slug. The renderer looks up that value to choose the React component.

deep_dive.title: Block definitions
deep_dive.body: Define blocks once and reference them where needed. Shared definitions keep the admin consistent and reduce the config sent to the client.

deep_dive.title: Validation
deep_dive.body: Use `minRows`, `maxRows`, and required fields to catch empty pages before they publish. A page builder without guardrails becomes a layout lottery.

deep_dive.title: Rendering
deep_dive.body: A registry keyed by `blockType` is enough for most teams. Unknown blocks should render nothing or a safe fallback, never crash the page.

lessons.title: Build a block inspector
lessons.outcome: Design a Payload block inspector that helps editors identify, reorder, and configure blocks without losing page context.
mental_model: **Blocks are authored structure.** The inspector should expose what a block is before exposing its fields.
**Position is content meaning.** Reordering must communicate where the block will land, not only provide arrows.
**Configuration is progressive.** Keep the overview compact and let editors open deeper settings when needed.

lessons.outcome: Create a Payload array-field editor that makes repeated items easy to add, reorder, duplicate, and remove.
mental_model: **Repeated fields need identity.** Every item should have a useful summary so editors can find it again.
**Mutation should preserve confidence.** Add, move, duplicate, and remove actions need immediate, specific feedback.
**Structure should survive narrow layouts.** Repeated items can stack while their controls remain reachable.

lessons.title: Build an access-control banner
lessons.outcome: Design a Payload access-control banner that explains draft, published, and restricted states without pretending the user can perform unavailable actions.
mental_model: **Access decisions shape actions.** The banner should reflect what Payload allows instead of rendering every button optimistically.
**Draft and published are different truths.** State labels should explain visibility and editability separately.
**The next action should be honest.** Link to request access, preview, or return to the list rather than showing a dead control.

lessons.title: Design a relationship picker
lessons.outcome: Make a Payload relationship field understandable by showing the selected document, search context, and removal action.
mental_model: **Relationships are content navigation.** The field should reveal what is linked, not only store an ID.
**Search needs context.** Show the collection and enough document metadata to distinguish similar records.
**Selection is reversible.** Make replacement and removal explicit so editors stay in control.

knowledge_check.question: What information best helps an editor distinguish related documents?

deep_dive.title: Relationship cardinality
deep_dive.body: One-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships change the selection model. The label should make that model visible to editors.

deep_dive.title: Admin ergonomics
deep_dive.body: Payload field components run inside an editor workflow. Preserve familiar labels, keyboard behavior, and clear save-state feedback.

deep_dive.title: Query context
deep_dive.body: A real relationship picker can use the collection's search fields and access rules. The UI should never imply that an inaccessible document can be selected.

lessons.title: Build a Payload pie chart
lessons.outcome: Turn Payload acquisition records into a responsive pie chart that explains each channel's share, with editable values and an intentional admin-to-frontend visual handoff.
mental_model: **Parts need a whole.** A pie chart is useful when each Payload channel contributes to one meaningful total.
**The row is the contract.** Labels, values, and units stay editable so the chart is never disconnected from CMS content.
**Responsive is a legend problem.** Keep slice colors, labels, percentages, and exact values understandable as the card narrows.

knowledge_check.question: When is a Payload pie chart a good choice?
options: When the rows are parts of one meaningful whole
When every category is an unrelated time series
When exact comparisons are the only goal
When the data has no labels
knowledge_check.explanation: A pie chart communicates composition: each labeled row should represent a share of the same total.

deep_dive.title: Parts of a whole
deep_dive.body: Pie slices communicate composition, not precise ranking. Use them for a small set of categories that share one total.

deep_dive.title: Legend as interface
deep_dive.body: The legend carries the exact values and labels that a slice cannot show by itself. Keep it readable and let it wrap on narrow screens.

deep_dive.title: CMS contract
deep_dive.body: Payload stores structured rows, while the pie renderer derives proportions at display time. Editing one value changes the whole composition.

lessons.title: Build a Payload doughnut chart
lessons.outcome: Design a responsive Payload doughnut chart that shows the balance between release states while keeping the total and segment labels visible.
mental_model: **The center creates context.** A doughnut leaves room for a total or headline metric.
**Segments need a shared measure.** Each Payload status must use the same unit before it can be compared as part of the whole.
**Responsive is not smaller desktop.** The ring can resize while the center total and legend preserve the message.

A decorative value with no connection to the rows

knowledge_check.explanation: The center gives the ring context, such as the total number of records represented by its segments.

deep_dive.title: A ring with a reason
deep_dive.body: The hollow center is useful space, not decoration. Use it for a total, percentage, or short statement that explains the segments.

deep_dive.title: Accessible composition

deep_dive.title: Responsive segments
deep_dive.body: A responsive doughnut changes its available size, not the underlying proportions. The normalized rows remain the source of truth.

lessons.title: Drafts, preview, publish
lessons.outcome: Move a component from draft to published, preview it before the public sees it, and make the state visible.
mental_model: **Draft and published are states, not copies.** A drafts-enabled collection keeps the working version separate from the public version.
**Preview is a live channel.** Payload streams form state to the preview route; you render the same components with the draft data.
**Access control is the door.** Public read access must exclude drafts; the UI should never be the only thing hiding them.

knowledge_check.question: What does `_status` control in a drafts-enabled collection?
options: Whether a document is a draft or published
knowledge_check.explanation: Payload adds `_status` to drafts-enabled documents. Public reads should filter to published documents, while editors and preview routes can read drafts.

deep_dive.title: Versions and drafts
deep_dive.body: Drafts keep a working copy; versions keep a history. Enable both when editors need to compare or restore, and make the published state explicit in the UI.

deep_dive.title: Live preview
deep_dive.body: Payload's live preview sends form state to an iframe with `postMessage`. The preview route uses the same components as the public page, so what editors see is what ships.

deep_dive.title: The access boundary
deep_dive.body: Hiding a draft in the UI is not security. Public read access must return a query that excludes drafts; the showcase should query published documents explicitly.

lessons.title: Capstone: the showcase
lessons.outcome: Ship a polished testimonial to the public showcase and verify it survives every device and state.
mental_model: **The showcase is a product surface.** It has a hierarchy, a filter model, and a quality bar; it is not a debug page.
**Polish is systems work.** Responsive layout, contrast, focus, and empty states are part of the component, not a final coat of paint.
**Publishing is a promise.** Once a component is public, it represents the course; check it before you flip the state.

options: The component has a unique animation
The layout survives mobile and contrast passes
The name is longer than the description
knowledge_check.explanation: Publishing is a quality gate. Responsive behavior and contrast are baseline checks; decoration is optional.

deep_dive.title: Responsive by construction
deep_dive.body: Use fluid widths, `minmax`, and wrapping instead of fixed pixel layouts. Test the component at 360px, 768px, and full width before publishing.

deep_dive.title: Content quality
deep_dive.body: A showcase is only as good as its weakest entry. Complete attributions, specific copy, and one clear idea per component make the gallery useful to the next learner.

deep_dive.title: Moderation
deep_dive.body: Learner-published does not mean unmoderated. The admin can feature, unpublish, or delete a submission; the public API only ever exposes published, public components.

lessons.title: Build a numeric data table
lessons.outcome: Create a small table of numbers, style it with the shared build controls, save it to Payload, and read the same rows in the Level 8 chart.
mental_model: **The form is the schema.** Title, caption, unit, and rows are the data contract the chart reads.
**Reuse the controls.** The same BuilderFields inputs and design tokens drive the form and the live table.
**Save, then fetch.** The table is stored in the CMS; Level 8 loads the newest saved table and turns it into a bar chart.
**Keep it small.** A short numeric table is easy to validate, reload, and chart.

lab.title: Save a table of numbers
lab.brief: Edit the rows and labels, adjust the design tokens, then save the table to Payload. The newest saved table becomes the saved-form chart in the Level 8 showcase.
checklist: Every row has a label and a number
The table title describes the data
The unit is visible
The design tokens still pass contrast
The table is saved in the CMS

content.title: Signups by channel
content.caption: A small numeric table saved in Payload and reused by the Level 8 chart.

hints: Use the Number rows list to add, remove, or reorder rows.
The chart uses the row labels as categories and the values as bars.
Save again to update the same table, or reset to start a new version.

lessons.takeaway: A small, validated table saved in Payload is enough data to drive a real chart without exposing the CMS credentials.

knowledge_check.question: Where should the Level 8 chart get the numbers from the form?
options: From the newest saved data-table component in Payload
From a hard-coded array in the chart component
From the browser's local storage only
knowledge_check.explanation: The form saves its rows in Payload. The Level 8 server loader reads the newest saved table, validates the rows, and passes a small chart-ready series to the browser.

deep_dive.title: Why store rows, not markup?
deep_dive.body: The builder saves the labels and numbers as structured content. The preview can change without losing the data, and the chart reads the same values instead of scraping the table.

deep_dive.title: One contract, two views
deep_dive.body: The form preview and the Level 8 chart both consume the same title, unit, and row objects. That keeps the data honest when either view changes.

deep_dive.title: Small data is still data
deep_dive.body: Validation belongs at the edge: require labels, finite numbers, and a bounded row count so a malformed table cannot break the chart.

lessons.title: Design a version history panel
lessons.outcome: Present Payload versions as a readable timeline with author, state, and a safe restore action.
mental_model: **A version is a decision point.** Show who changed what and when before offering restore.
**Draft and published are different states.** Editors need to know which version is public.
**Restore is reversible in practice.** Make the action explicit and explain that it creates a new draft.

lab.title: Build the version timeline
lab.brief: Turn the list of revisions into a useful Payload admin panel. Distinguish published and draft versions, show authorship, and make restore feedback visible.
checklist: Versions are ordered newest first
Published state is textual
Each version shows author and time
Restore action explains its result
The current version is identifiable
hints: Use a timeline or stacked list so chronology is obvious.
Do not communicate published state with color alone.
Restoring should say what happens next: it creates a new draft.

starter.html:
Versions

Updated headlineToday · Draft
First published versionYesterday · Published

solution.html:
Post · Story

Version history

3 versions
  1. Updated headlineSam Rivera · 2 minutes ago
    Current draft
  2. Reviewed by editorialSam Rivera · Yesterday
    Published
  3. First versionAlex Chen · Monday
    Draft

lessons.takeaway: Version history is more than a date list: it gives Payload editors confidence to experiment without losing the published story.

knowledge_check.question: What should restoring an older Payload version communicate?
options: It silently deletes every newer version
It creates a new draft from the selected version
knowledge_check.explanation: A safe restore preserves history and gives the editor a draft to review before publishing.

deep_dive.title: Versions versus revisions
deep_dive.body: A revision records a saved state. A versioning UI should make the saved state, author, and publication status easy to inspect.

deep_dive.title: Editorial confidence
deep_dive.body: Clear restore feedback lowers the cost of experimentation while keeping publication as a deliberate step.

deep_dive.title: Chronology
deep_dive.body: Newest-first ordering matches editorial workflows, while a visible current marker prevents confusion between the active draft and an older snapshot.

lessons.title: Build a live preview toolbar
lessons.outcome: Design a Payload live-preview toolbar that makes draft status, viewport choice, and refresh behavior explicit.
mental_model: **Preview is not publish.** The toolbar must make draft context unmistakable.
**Viewport is a test tool.** Switching widths helps catch layout regressions before an editor publishes.
**Refresh should explain itself.** Show when the preview is stale and what action updates it.

lab.title: Compose the preview controls
lab.brief: Build a compact live-preview toolbar for a Payload page. Show that the editor is viewing a draft, provide viewport controls, and make refresh feedback visible.
checklist: Draft context is unmistakable
Viewport controls have accessible labels
Active viewport is visually and textually clear
Refresh action gives feedback
Toolbar remains usable below 480px
hints: Use a badge and text; do not rely on a yellow background to mean draft.
Icon-only viewport buttons need aria-labels and visible active state.
A small status message can explain that the preview was refreshed.

solution.html: Live previewDraft · not published

lessons.takeaway: A live preview earns trust when draft status, viewport context, and refresh state are always visible.

knowledge_check.question: What must a live-preview toolbar distinguish?
knowledge_check.explanation: Editors need to know whether they are looking at unpublished draft content or the public page.

deep_dive.title: Preview URLs
deep_dive.body: Payload preview URLs can include draft context and a secret or signed mechanism. The toolbar should reinforce that context instead of hiding it.

deep_dive.title: Viewport testing
deep_dive.body: Desktop and mobile toggles are simple, but they make responsive review part of the editorial workflow rather than an afterthought.

deep_dive.title: Stale previews
deep_dive.body: When data changes asynchronously, a visible refresh or updated-at message helps editors understand whether they are seeing the latest draft.
